sections.learningObjectives:
- Define negligence and malpractice and identify the elements of duty, breach, causation, and damages.
- Explain how staying within scope of practice and working under supervision reduce the risk of harm and liability.
- Describe the medical office's duty of care to protect patients and their health information.
- Identify everyday error-prevention practices, including verification, documentation, and privacy safeguards.
- Describe incident reporting, including what to document, how to report promptly, and its role in quality improvement.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Negligence is like a lifeguard who stops watching the pool and someone gets hurt because of it; it is carelessness that causes real harm, not just any small mistake.

### Question 2

Negligence is anyone being careless; malpractice is a professional, like a doctor or assistant, being careless at their job in a way that hurts someone.

### Question 3

To show someone was careless, you need four puzzle pieces: they had a job to be careful, they messed up, the mess-up caused a problem, and someone was actually hurt.

### Question 4

A duty of care is like the promise a bus driver makes to drive safely so passengers do not get hurt; it means being reasonably careful for others.

### Question 5

Keeping a patient's private health details safe is like keeping a friend's secret; it is a promise of care, not an extra favor.

### Question 6

Breaching a duty is like ignoring the 'wash your hands' rule at a restaurant; skipping a required safety step breaks the promise to be careful.

### Question 7

Causation is like proving that the spilled water, and not something else, is what made the floor slippery and caused the fall.

### Question 8

Damages are the 'ouch' that can be measured, like a broken arm or a lost wallet, not just being annoyed.

### Question 9

The standard of care is like the 'good driver' standard: you are judged against what a careful, sensible driver would do, not what a race car champion could do.

### Question 10

Professionals, like trained assistants, are held to the 'good assistant' standard, just as a plumber is held to the 'good plumber' standard.

### Question 11

You can break a friend's phone by being careless even if you never meant to; that is what negligence is about.

### Question 12

An intentional tort is pushing someone on purpose; negligence is accidentally bumping into them because you were not watching where you were going.

### Question 13

Being careful at work means doing the things you were trained to do, the right way, not trying everything at top speed.

### Question 14

The office promises to look out for every patient, just like a school promises to keep every student safe, not just the ones whose parents donate money.

### Question 15

The breach is the moment the secret was let out; the hurt feelings and lost money are separate pieces of the puzzle.

### Question 16

Following the rulebook is like following a recipe exactly; it shows you did things the careful, accepted way.

### Question 17

Writing down what you did is like keeping a receipt; it proves what happened if there is ever a question.

### Question 18

Keeping secrets is the office's promise; breaking it is the kind of carelessness that can get the office in trouble.

### Question 19

Checking who someone is before handing over private papers is like checking ID before giving a package to the right person.

### Question 20

Foreseeable means you could guess it might happen, like knowing a spilled drink could make someone slip.

### Question 21

When you are not sure, asking is the grown-up, careful move, like asking for directions instead of driving the wrong way.

### Question 22

The careless part was leaving the private paper out in the open, even if no one meant any harm.

### Question 23

Staying in your lane is like a goalie staying in the goal area instead of trying to play every position; it keeps everyone safer.

### Question 24

Your allowed tasks come from the official rulebook and your boss's instructions, not from what you or a patient would like.

### Question 25

A supervisor is like a lifeguard watching swimmers; the extra eyes help stop small problems before they become big ones.

### Question 26

If someone asks you to do a job you were never taught and are not allowed to do, the smart move is to say so and ask the boss.

### Question 27

If a friend asks you a question only a doctor should answer, the careful thing is to send them to the doctor, not make something up.

### Question 28

Only someone with a license gets to decide what is wrong; the assistant's job is to help gather and relay information, not to be the doctor.

### Question 29

When a question needs a doctor's answer, pass it to the doctor right away instead of guessing.

### Question 30

Minimum necessary means sharing only the little bit of information you need, like opening only the page you need instead of the whole book.

### Question 31

Just because you have a key to the file cabinet does not mean you may open any drawer you like; you may open only the one your job needs.

### Question 32

You may share a secret only when the person who owns it says yes in writing, or when the rules clearly allow it.

### Question 33

You would not fly a plane just because the pilot is busy and a passenger offers instructions; you wait for someone who is trained and allowed to do it.

### Question 34

Before taking on a new chore, check that you have been taught how and are allowed to do it, like checking you can actually swim before jumping in.

### Question 35

The rules at your house might be different from your friend's house, so you ask the grown-ups in each place what is allowed.

### Question 36

Being properly trained is like having a driver's license and lessons before getting on the road; it keeps you and others safe.

### Question 37

When you are not sure if you are allowed to do something, check the rulebook and ask the boss before you do it.

### Question 38

Doing a chore the way the boss showed you and writing down what you did is like keeping a clean, signed checklist.

### Question 39

The assistant is like the helper who hands tools and follows the builder's plan, not the one who decides how to build the house.

### Question 40

Staying in your lane keeps you from doing things you have not practiced, which is what keeps everyone safe.

### Question 41

Writing things down clearly is like leaving a clear note so the next person does not mix up the details.

### Question 42

Before handing a package to someone, you check they are really the person who should get it, not just someone who says so.

### Question 43

If you are not sure what someone said, repeat it back so they can fix it, like repeating a phone number to make sure you got it right.

### Question 44

If you are not sure how to spell a word, look it up instead of guessing, just like checking a dictionary.

### Question 45

A checklist is like a pilot's before-takeoff list; it makes sure nothing important is forgotten.

### Question 46

Before hitting send, check the address twice, like double-checking the envelope before mailing a private letter.

### Question 47

You would not throw a private letter in the public trash; you shred it so no one can read it.

### Question 48

Leaving your desk is like leaving your locker open; you close and lock it so no one peeks.

### Question 49

Passwords are like your own locker key; if you share it, no one can tell who opened the locker.

### Question 50

It is like making a repair company sign a promise to keep your things safe while they fix your house.

### Question 51

The Notice is like a handout that explains the office's 'house rules' for keeping your private information safe.

### Question 52

You are allowed to read and get a copy of your own report card, but not your classmate's.

### Question 53

If your school file has a mistake, you can ask to have it fixed through the office, not scribble it out yourself.

### Question 54

It is like asking for a list of everyone the office told your secret to, so you can see where your information went.

### Question 55

If you think someone broke the rules about your private information, there is an official place you can tell, like the principal's office.

### Question 56

De-identified means taking your name, address, and birthday off the paper so no one can tell whose paper it is.

### Question 57

Private conversations happen behind a closed door, not in the middle of the lunchroom.

### Question 58

If you spill something, you tell a grown-up right away so it can be cleaned up before someone slips.

### Question 59

Checking a name and birthday is like checking a name on a test before writing on it, so you do not write on the wrong paper.

### Question 60

Administrative safeguards are like the school's rules and training that make sure only the right people get into the right rooms.

### Question 61

An incident report is like a note explaining what went wrong so everyone can fix the problem, not a note to get someone in trouble.

### Question 62

You write an incident report for something surprising and possibly harmful, like a slip, not for an ordinary, safe day.

### Question 63

Write down just the facts, like a reporter: who, what, when, and where, without saying whose fault it is.

### Question 64

Write what you saw and when you saw it, like 'the cup was on the edge at 3 o'clock,' not 'someone is always clumsy.'

### Question 65

Write down what happened right away, because you remember the details best when they just happened.

### Question 66

A near miss is like almost tripping on a loose rug; you tell someone so the rug gets fixed before anyone actually falls.

### Question 67

If you mail a letter to the wrong house, you tell a grown-up right away instead of pretending it did not happen.

### Question 68

The note goes to the person in charge whose job is to fix problems, not to everyone in town.

### Question 69

A just culture is like a team where players can say 'I dropped the ball' so the coach can fix the play, instead of everyone hiding mistakes.

### Question 70

The incident report is the office's private note to itself, kept separate from the patient's file, not posted for everyone.

### Question 71

Tell your teacher or the person in charge first when you see a problem, not the whole class.

### Question 72

One note is the office writing down what happened; the other is a patient telling the office they are unhappy.

### Question 73

If a secret gets out, the office has to tell the person whose secret it was, not pretend nothing happened.

### Question 74

Write down what you actually saw and did, like a careful diary, not guesses about people's feelings.

### Question 75

Lots of little notes can show a pattern, like realizing every slip happens on the same step, so you fix that step.

### Question 76

The four pieces line up like a chain: duty, mistake, the mistake caused the hurt, and the hurt is real.

### Question 77

Negligence is skipping the steps you were taught; an act of nature or a surprise breakdown is a different kind of problem.

### Question 78

Risk management is like a parent checking the playground for broken swings before the kids play, to stop problems before they happen.

### Question 79

Just because a famous person's file is interesting does not mean you may open it; it is still their private file.

### Question 80

A friend asking you to do something you have not been trained for does not make it safe, like being asked to drive a truck without lessons.

### Question 81

If you are handed a task with no instructions, ask the person who gave it to you what to do instead of making it up.

### Question 82

If someone almost slips, you check on them and mop the floor right away so no one actually falls.

### Question 83

Pointing your private papers toward a crowded room breaks the promise to keep them safe, even if you did not mean to.

### Question 84

Checking the name and birthday is like making sure you hand the right lunchbox to the right kid.

### Question 85

Being allowed to do something does not always mean it is the kind thing to do; good helpers follow both the rules and their conscience.
